ἀμέτρως ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ ὑπερφέρειν παντὸς νοῦ «αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς» καλέσας μυστικώτατα. 15.52 ὅτι γὰρ παντὸς χρόνου, ὃν ἂν νοήσῃ τις πολλὰ κυκλεύσας τῇ διανοίᾳ, ἀπεράντως ἀνώτατος καὶ ποσότητος πάσης ἀσυγκρίτως ἀμείνων καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἀπερινόητος καὶ πάντοθεν ἄποπτος εἰς ἅπαν καθέστηκεν–αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν περιβαλὼν καὶ οὐδὲν ἑαυτοῦ ἔξωθεν ἔχων–, καὶ παραχωρεῖ τῷ τοσούτῳ αὐτοῦ ἀκαταλήπτῳ καὶ ἡ ἀγγέλων πληθύς, καὶ πᾶς οὐρανίων ταγμάτων δῆμος ἐκβοῶσιν ὡδί· ὁ μὲν ∆αυῒδ ἐν ιζʹ ψαλμῷ· «ἔθετο σκότος ἀποκρυφὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ κύκλῳ αὐτοῦ ἡ σκηνὴ αὐτοῦ», ἡ δὲ ᾠδὴ Ἀμβακούμ· «ἐκάλυψεν οὐρανοὺς ἡ ἀρετὴ αὐτοῦ», 15.53 ὁ δὲ Ματθαῖος «οὐδείς» φησίν «γινώσκει τὸν υἱόν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ, οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα τις ἐπιγι νώσκει, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός». 15.54 Τὸ μὲν γὰρ τεχθὲν παρὰ τῆς κτίσεως κατὰ κοινωνίαν ἄλλου πρὸς ἄλλο γεγέννηται καὶ οὐ συμφυὲς τῷ γεννήσαντι, οὐδὲ τέλειον εὐθὺς καὶ ἀπαθῶς ἐξελήλυθεν· 15.55 ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς θεότητος τὸ ἔμπαλιν. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἡ κτίσις τοιῶσδε, ὁ γενεσιουργὸς ἐναντίως καὶ οὐχ ὁμοίως τῶν ἰδίων ποιημάτων, ἀλλ' ὡς οἶδεν ταῦτα μόνη ἡ μακαρία τριάς. 15.56 οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀκατάληπτος, εἰ κατελαμβάνετο, οὐδὲ μυστήριον, εἰ ἐγινώσκετο, οὐδὲ θεῖον, εἰ ἐχωρεῖτο, οὐδὲ δημιουργὸς πάντων, εἰ ἀπὸ χρόνου, οὐδὲ ἀσύνθετος καὶ ἀμερής, εἰ πρὸς τὰ σώματα. 15.57 καθάπερ γὰρ 10 ἀκούοντες περὶ τοῦ πατρός «ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος σὺ εἶ» καί «ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν ἡ ἀλήθεια αὐτοῦ» οὐχ ὅρους τιθέαμεν αὐτῷ, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀΐδιον πιστεύομεν· οὐ γὰρ ὁμῆλιξ αὐτῷ ὁ αἰών, ὡσαύτως περί τε τοῦ υἱοῦ καῖ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος φρονεῖν ὀφείλομεν, ἐπὶ γὰρ τῆς πάντων ἐπικρατούσης μιᾶς φύσεως, εἰς ἣν αὗται αἱ πάντιμοι ὑποστάσεις. 15.58 τὰ ἴσα μελῳδεῖ καὶ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ· «σὺ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σοῦ οὐκ ἐκ λείψουσιν». καὶ εἰ μὴ μικρὸν τὸ περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς γεγράφθαι «ὁ ὑπάρχων πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων», οὐ μικρὸν οὐδὲ τὸ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ χρησμῳδηθέν, ὅτι «προαιώνιος θεός». δῆλον δ' ὡς ἀπερινόητος, καθὰ δειχθήσεται οὐ πολλῷ ὕστερον. καὶ καθὰ ὁ πατήρ «ἔχει ἀθανασίαν», μᾶλλον δὲ αὐτός ἐστιν ἡ ἀθανασία, οὕτως ὁ υἱός ἐστιν «ζωὴ αἰώνιος», ἔστιν δὲ τὸ αὐτό. 15.59 Καὶ ὥσπερ ὁ πατήρ «εἷς θεός» εἴρηται, οὕτω ὁ υἱὸς κέκληται μονογενής, θεός, λόγος καί «εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός». 15.60 καὶ ὡς Ἰάκωβος περὶ αὐτοῦ γράφει 15.60 «εἷς ἐστιν ὁ νομοθέτης καὶ κριτής, ὁ μόνος σώζειν δυνάμενος», οὕτω τὸ πνεῦμα παρὰ Παύλου Κορινθίοις καὶ Ἐφεσίοις γράψαντος ὕμνηται «ἕν» καί «τὸ αὐτό» καὶ μόνον, καὶ μόνον, ἵνα καὶ αὐτῷ τούτῳ τῷ ὡσανεὶ ἀριθμῷ, ἵν' οὕτω λεχθῇ, δείκνυνται φέρουσαι αἱ μακάριαι ὑποστάσεις αὗται τὸ ἑναδικὸν ἤτοι μοναδικὸν τῆς πατρικῆς θεότητος. 15.61 καὶ εἰ ἐπὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀληθὲς τό «ὁ θεὸς καὶ κύριος», ἀψευδὲς καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος. 15.62 Ὡς γὰρ ἐπεμνήσθημεν πολλαχοῦ, ἥ τε πρεσβυτέρα διαθήκη τὴν ἰσοτιμίαν φυλάξασα διελάλησεν· «εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου», καί «ἔβρεξεν κύριος παρὰ κυρίου», καί «ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ τὸν ἄνθρωπον», καί «τίς θεὸς πάρεξ τοῦ κυρίου καί τίς θεὸς πλὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν;» 15.63 Καὶ ἐν τῇ νέᾳ δὲ διαθήκῃ ὁ μὲν Ἰωάννης ἔφη, ἅπερ ἤδη ἐλέχθη. ὁ δὲ Θωμᾶς «ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου», καὶ ὁ Παῦλος «ὁ δὲ κύριος τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν, οὗ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα κυρίου, ἐκεῖ ἐλευθερία», καὶ πάλιν. «καθάπερ ἀπὸ κυρίου πνεύματος» καὶ «δῴη κύριος εὑρεῖν ἔλεος παρὰ κυρίου τῷ Ὀνησιφόρου οἴκῳ». ὁ δὲ Ἰώβ· «πνεῦμα θεῖον τὸ ποιῆσάν με», καὶ «πνεῦμα θεῖον τὸ περιόν μοι ἐν ῥισίν». 15.64 Ταὐτὸν δέ ἐστιν τῇ γραφῇ λέξαι «θεῖον» ἤ «θεόν», ὡς διδάσκουσιν Παῦλος μὲν Ῥωμαίοις γράφων· «ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θεότης», αἱ δὲ Πράξεις· «οὐκ ὀφείλομεν νομίζειν χρυσῷ ἢ ἀργύρῳ ἢ λίθῳ, χαράγματι τέχνης ἢ ἐν θυμήσεως ἀνθρωπίνης, τὸ θεῖον εἶναι ὅμοιον», ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ ἐπιστολῇ· «ἵνα διὰ τούτων γένησθε θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως». 15.65 Καὶ ὃν τρόπον ὁ πατὴρ ἀκατάληπτος, οὕτω καὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ὁ πλοῦτος ἀνεξιχνίαστος κατὰ τὸν Παῦλον τυγχάνει ὤν. φησὶν γάρ· «ἐμοὶ τῷ ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἐδόθη ἡ χάρις, εὐαγγελίζε σθαι ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι τὸν ἀνεξιχνίαστον πλοῦτον τοῦ Χριστοῦ». ἀλλὰ καὶ «τῆς μεγαλωσύνης αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν πέρας» οὔτε «τῆς συνέσεως ἀριθμός» κατὰ τὸν ∆αυΐδ, οὔτε «τῆς εἰρήνης ὅριον» κατὰ Ἠσαΐαν,
pass_a_gloss: [15.50 continued from the previous section: 'and he is a man, and who] will know him?', in place of 'no one'. 15.51 And concerning the above [birth]: 'and his generation who will recount, because his life is lifted from the earth?', having called most mystically the begetting 'generation', the existence 'life', and the being lifted up exceedingly without measure from the earth and surpassing every mind 'is lifted from the earth'. 15.52 For that, of every time which someone might think of having circled much with the understanding, he has been established boundlessly highest, and incomparably better than every quantity, and in substance not to be thought around, and from all sides out of sight entirely (himself having encompassed himself and having nothing of himself outside), and [that] both the multitude of angels gives way to so great an incomprehensibility of his, and all the people of the heavenly ranks, they cry aloud thus: David in the seventeenth [Greek numbering] psalm: 'he set darkness [as] his concealment, and round about him his tent'; and the ode of Habakkuk: 'his excellence covered heavens'; 15.53 and Matthew says: 'no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone fully know the Father except the Son'. 15.54 For the thing brought forth by creation has been begotten according to a communion of one toward another, and not grown-together with the one who begot, nor has it come out perfect straightway and impassibly; 15.55 but in the case of the Godhead the reverse. For since the creation [is] of such sort, the author of coming-to-be [is] oppositely and not like his own makings, but as the blessed Trinity alone knows these things. 15.56 For [he would be] neither incomprehensible, if he were comprehended, nor a mystery, if he were known, nor divine, if he were contained, nor craftsman of all, if from time, nor uncompounded and partless, if [he were] toward bodies. 15.57 For just as, hearing concerning the Father 'from the age and up to the age you are' and 'up to the clouds his truth', we do not place boundaries for him, but we believe the everlastingness; for the age is not of like age with him; in the same way we are bound to think concerning both the Son and the Holy Spirit; for [it is] in the case of the one nature that prevails over all, into which [are] these all-honoured hypostases. 15.58 It sings the equal things concerning the Son too: 'you are the same, and your years will not give out'. And if [it is] not small that it has been written concerning the Father 'the one existing before the ages', not small either is the thing oracularly sung concerning his Son, that [he is] 'God before the ages'. And [it is] clear that [he is] not to be thought around, as will be shown not much later. And according as the Father 'has immortality', or rather himself is the immortality, so the Son is 'eternal life', and it is the same. 15.59 And just as the Father has been spoken of as 'one God', so the Son has been called only-begotten, God, Word, and 'one Lord Jesus Christ'. 15.60 And as James writes concerning him [the number 15.60 is printed twice]: 'one is the lawgiver and judge, the one alone able to save', so the Spirit, by Paul having written to Corinthians and Ephesians, has been hymned 'one' and 'the same' and only, and only [repeated], so that by this very as-it-were number, so that it may be said thus, these blessed hypostases are shown bearing the one-ness or single-ness of the paternal Godhead. 15.61 And if in the case of the Father the [title] 'the God and Lord' [is] true, [it is] unlying also in the case of his Son and the Spirit. 15.62 For as we have made mention in many places, the older covenant, having guarded the equality of honour, spoke out: 'the Lord said to my Lord', and 'the Lord rained from the Lord', and 'God made the human being according to the image of God', and 'who [is] God except the Lord, and who [is] God besides our God?' 15.63 And in the new covenant John said the things that were already spoken. And Thomas: 'my Lord and my God', and Paul: 'and the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord, there freedom', and again: 'just as from the Lord Spirit', and 'may the Lord give to find mercy from the Lord to the house of Onesiphorus'. And Job: 'divine spirit the one having made me', and 'divine spirit the one remaining for me in nostrils'. 15.64 And it is the same for the Scripture to say 'divine' or 'God', as they teach: Paul writing to Romans: 'both his everlasting power and Godhead', and the Acts: 'we ought not to suppose the divine to be like to gold or silver or stone, to an engraving of craft and of human thought', and Peter in the second letter: 'so that through these you may become sharers of divine nature'. 15.65 And in the way the Father [is] incomprehensible, so also the wealth of Christ happens to be untraceable according to Paul. For he says: 'to me, the more-least of all human beings, the grace was given, to proclaim good news among the nations, the untraceable wealth of Christ'. But also 'of his greatness there is no limit', nor 'of the understanding a number', according to David, nor 'of the peace a boundary', according to Isaiah, [continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … will know him?” (Jeremiah 17:9), meaning “no one.” And about the birth above: “And who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken up from the earth” (Isaiah 53:8). In the most mystical way he called the begetting “generation,” his existence “life,” and his being lifted beyond all measure above the earth and surpassing every mind, “is taken up from the earth.”

For he stands boundlessly higher than any time that one might conceive after circling long in thought, incomparably greater than every quantity, in his substance beyond conceiving, and on every side wholly out of sight, encompassing himself and having nothing of himself outside. Before an incomprehensibility so great the multitude of angels gives way, and so does the whole people of the heavenly ranks. All this they proclaim aloud: David in the eighteenth Psalm, “He made darkness his hiding place, and round about him was his tent” (Psalm 18:11); the Song of Habakkuk, “His excellence covered the heavens” (Habakkuk 3:3); and Matthew, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11:27).

For what is born from creation is begotten through the union of one with another; it is not inseparably one with its begetter, nor does it come forth perfect at once and without passion. With the Godhead it is the reverse. Since creation is of this kind, the Author of all that comes to be is the opposite, and not like his own works, but as the blessed Trinity alone knows. For he would not be incomprehensible if he were comprehended, nor a mystery if he were known, nor divine if he could be contained, nor the Maker of all if he were from time, nor uncompounded and without parts if he were of the order of bodies.

When we hear it said of the Father, “From age to age you are” (Psalm 90:2), and “His truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 57:10), we do not set limits to him, but believe that he is eternal; for the age is not his contemporary. In the same way we ought to think of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, for we are speaking of the one nature that rules over all, to which these all-honoured hypostases belong.

The same is sung of the Son: “You are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:27; Hebrews 1:12). And if it is no small thing that it is written of the Father, “He who exists before the ages” (Psalm 55:19), no small thing either is what was spoken in prophecy of his Son, that he is “God before the ages” (Psalm 74:12). It is plain that he is beyond conceiving, as will be shown not much later. And just as the Father “has immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), or rather is himself immortality, so the Son is “eternal life” (1 John 5:20); and that is the same thing.

And just as the Father is called “one God,” so the Son is called Only-begotten, God, Word, and “one Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6). And as James writes of him, “There is one lawgiver and judge, who alone is able to save” (James 4:12), so the Spirit is hymned by Paul, writing to the Corinthians and the Ephesians, as “one” and “the same” (1 Corinthians 12:11; Ephesians 4:4), and as only, so that by this very quasi-number, if one may put it so, these blessed hypostases are shown to bear the oneness, that is, the singleness, of the Father’s Godhead. And if “God and Lord” is true of the Father, it is just as free of falsehood of his Son and of the Spirit.

For, as we have recalled in many places, the older covenant, guarding their equal honour, declared: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Psalm 110:1); and “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Genesis 19:24); and “God made man according to the image of God” (Genesis 1:27); and “Who is God except the Lord, and who is God besides our God?” (Psalm 18:31). And in the new covenant John said what has already been quoted; Thomas said, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28); and Paul, “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17); and again, “as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18); and “May the Lord grant the household of Onesiphorus to find mercy from the Lord” (2 Timothy 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:18). And Job: “The divine Spirit that made me” (Job 33:4), and “the divine Spirit that is still in my nostrils” (Job 27:3).

It is the same thing for Scripture to say “divine” or “God,” as they teach: Paul, writing to the Romans, “his eternal power and Godhead” (Romans 1:20); the Acts, “We ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image carved by art and human thought” (Acts 17:29); and Peter in his second letter, “that through these you may become sharers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4).

And just as the Father is incomprehensible, so too, according to Paul, the riches of Christ are beyond tracing. For he says, “To me, the very least of all people, this grace was given, to preach among the nations the untraceable riches of Christ” (Ephesians 3:8). And more: “Of his greatness there is no end” (Psalm 145:3), nor “of understanding any number” (Psalm 147:5), as David says, nor “of peace any bound” (Isaiah 9:7), as Isaiah says …

choices.issue: Old draft reversed and garbled clauses
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English rendered περὶ τῆς ἄνω (the birth above) as 'Regarding the divine'; garbled 15.52 ('because He has become everything to all', 'better in quantity'); made 15.54 'not of the same nature' for οὐ συμφυές; reversed 15.55 (ἔμπαλιν, the reverse, as 'the same applies'), the first clause of 15.56 and 15.58 ('although … is small' for no small thing); made 15.57 'those hearing say' and 'the age does not dwell with Him'; broke 15.58 into a fragment paragraph ('Not merely immortality'); turned ὕμνηται into 'according to the hymns written by Paul'; made 2 Timothy 1:16-18 'may the Lord find grace for Onesiphorus's house' and Job 27:3 'surrounds me with rays'; rendered συνέσεως as 'wisdom'; and used bracket fillers '[said]', '[say]' and 'unto'. References: Genesis 1:26 corrected to Genesis 1:27 (the clause quotes 'God made man according to the image of God'); '(Matt 11:27)', '(Ps 90:2)', '(Ps 102:27)' written out; Psalm 36:5 replaced by Psalm 57:10 (truth to the clouds); Jeremiah 17:9, Isaiah 53:8, Psalm 18:11, Habakkuk 3:3, Hebrews 1:12, Psalm 74:12 (LXX 73:12, which Didymus reads προαιώνιος, as in 15.89), 1 Timothy 6:16, 1 John 5:20, 1 Corinthians 8:6, 12:11, Ephesians 4:4, Genesis 19:24, Psalm 18:31, 2 Corinthians 3:18, 2 Timothy 1:16, 1:18, Job 33:4, 27:3, Psalm 145:3, 147:5 and Isaiah 9:7 added.

choices.why: The section opens inside the quotation begun in u03-open (LXX Jeremiah 17:9, 'and he is a man, and who will know him?'). Only this section's words are translated, with a leading ellipsis.

choices.english: is taken up from the earth
choices.why: αἴρω means both 'take away' (the sense of Isaiah 53:8) and 'lift up'; Didymus reads it as lifted above the earth, so 'taken up' keeps both.

choices.term: ὅτι γὰρ … καθέστηκεν … καὶ παραχωρεῖ … ἐκβοῶσιν ὡδί
choices.english: For he stands … gives way … All this they proclaim aloud: David …
choices.why: The ὅτι clause states what the witnesses proclaim; the subjects of ἐκβοῶσιν are David, the Song of Habakkuk and Matthew, listed next. The long period is split into three English sentences.
Greek (LXX) Psalm 17 is Psalm 18 in English numbering; the verse is Psalm 18:11.

choices.english: not inseparably one with its begetter
choices.why: συμφυής is 'grown together'; a creature's offspring shares its parent's kind but is a separate being. The old 'not of the same nature' said the opposite of Didymus' point.

choices.english: if he were of the order of bodies
choices.why: Elliptical: 'if [he stood] in relation to bodies', i.e. ranked with them.

choices.term: οὐ γὰρ ὁμῆλιξ αὐτῷ ὁ αἰών
choices.english: for the age is not his contemporary
choices.why: ὁμῆλιξ is 'of the same age': God is older than the age itself.

choices.term: εἰς ἣν αὗται αἱ πάντιμοι ὑποστάσεις
choices.english: to which these all-honoured hypostases belong
choices.why: The clause has no verb; 'belong' supplies the least English needs. Not bracketed: the sense is plain from εἰς ἥν.

choices.english: The same is sung of the Son
choices.why: The verb has no named subject (Scripture or the psalmist); the passive avoids supplying one.
Indicative after ἵνα in the copy-text; read as result.

choices.english: the oneness, that is, the singleness
choices.why: ἤτοι here explains, it does not offer an alternative.

choices.english: that is still in my nostrils
choices.why: περίειμι, 'remain, survive' (LXX Job 27:3); the old 'surrounds me with rays' misread it.
Double comparative of 'least' (as in Ephesians 3:8); Didymus has 'of all people' where Paul has 'of all the saints'.

choices.term: 15.60 … 15.60; καὶ μόνον, καὶ μόνον; ἐπιγι νώσκει; ἐκ λείψουσιν; εὐαγγελίζε σθαι; ἢ ἐν θυμήσεως; 10 ἀκούοντες
choices.why: Copy-text debris: the paragraph number 15.60 printed twice, 'and only' repeated (dittography, translated once), words split by line breaks, ἢ ἐν θυμήσεως read as ἐνθυμήσεως (Acts 17:29), and the printed line number '10' in 15.57 skipped.
